To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

when feeding less-filing diets to dairy cows with a high intake of forage containing a high proportion of legume forages, reducing dietary N concentrations can reduce the extent to increase N excretion.

the efficiency of N use by dairy cows is greater for diets with large proportions of legumes than for diets with large portions of nonlegumes, especially when the cows are fed at a high level of intake.
the response of N utilization to increasing DMI depends on the N content of the diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of dietary forage family on the response of N digestion and utilization to changes in feed intake.
the effect of preliminary feed consumption on the responses to diets differing in the family of the forage.
the effect of preliminary feed consumption on responses to diets differing in forage family.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of forage family on responses to N in diets fed to high-producing dairy cows is affected by the level of feed intake.
preliminary feed intake affects responses to alfalfa and orchardgrass diets in dairy cows by interacting with the digestibility of N in these forages.

as intake increased, cows on AL responded more than cows on OG, but as intake increased for AL, a decreasing proportion was digested and/or used for milk production or body tissue growth, indicating that reducing dietary CP content could increase N efficiency.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of forage family on N utilization depends on the level of N intake and that preliminary intake level affects the response of N utilization to changes in N intake.
the efficiency of N digestion and utilization is affected by forage family and by the interaction between forage family and pVDMI.
when feeding high-producing cows diets with large proportions of legumes, the efficiency of N digestion and utilization increases as intake increases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

when feeding less filling diets, such as large proportions of legumes, to cows, reducing dietary CP concentration could increase the proportion of N intake that is digested and utilized and reduce the extent that greater DMI leads greater N excretion.
the response of dairy cows to changes in dietary N concentration and forage family is dependent on the level of intake.

when feeding less-filler diets, such as diets high in legumes, to high-producing dairy cows, reducing dietary CP concentration may increase the efficiency of CP utilization and reduce the magnitude of the increase in CP excretion as DMI increases.
